canonical_name: Wallace H. Coulter 1953 Impedance Particle/Cell Counting Patent (Coulter Principle)
creator: Wallace H. Coulter (assigned later to Coulter Electronics, now Beckman Coulter / Danaher)
disclosure_citation: Coulter, W.H. US patent application filed 1949-10-20, US2656508A issued 1953-10-20, 'Means for counting particles suspended in a fluid'; Coulter, W.H. 'High speed automatic blood cell counter and cell size analyzer,' Proc. National Electronics Conference vol. 12 pp. 1034-1042 (1956)
end_application: automated cell counting (RBC, WBC, PLT in human and veterinary hematology); particle size analysis (industrial powders, paints, pharmaceutical APIs); foundational technology for ALL impedance-based hematology analyzers (Beckman Coulter, Sysmex, Mindray, IDEXX, Abbott Cell-Dyn, Nihon Kohden, etc.)
fabrication_method: precision-drilled aperture (~50-200 µm in original; 50-100 µm typical for blood cells; sub-µm for nanoparticle Coulter variants today) in a glass or sapphire wafer between two electrolyte chambers
flow_regime: constant-current or constant-voltage applied across aperture; particles suspended in electrolyte are pulled through aperture by pressure or flow; each particle displaces electrolyte volume equal to its own volume, momentarily increasing aperture impedance, producing a voltage pulse whose amplitude is proportional to particle volume
notable_capabilities: volume-resolved single-particle counting
throughput thousands of particles/second
electrolyte-conductivity-only requirement (no labels, no optics required)
extension to sub-micron via tunable resistive pulse sensing (TRPS, npore Coulter variant)
prior_art_notes: Discloses the foundational electrical-sensing-zone (Coulter principle) particle/cell counting technique: an electrolyte-filled chamber is divided by a small aperture (microfluidic constriction) bridged by an applied DC current; particles passing through the aperture displace electrolyte volume, momentarily increasing aperture impedance and producing voltage pulses whose amplitude is proportional to particle volume. Anticipates: ALL subsequent impedance-based microfluidic cell/particle counters (Coulter Counter Z series, all hematology analyzers using impedance, sub-µm 'tunable resistive pulse sensing' nanopore variants, microfluidic on-chip impedance cytometry). The 1953 patent expired in 1971 (17-year US term at the time), placing the foundational technique in the public domain — but downstream design improvements (sapphire apertures, hybrid optical-impedance, sweep-flow geometry) remain patented in modern instruments. This entry serves as the historical anchor making clear that any modern microfluidic impedance counter has 70+ years of expired-patent prior art to draw on.
sources: Coulter, W.H. Proc. National Electronics Conference 12:1034-1042 (1956)
Graham, M.D. 'The Coulter Principle: Foundation of an Industry,' JALA 8(6):72-81 (2003)
substrate_material: glass aperture (originally drilled in mica or glass); electrolyte (saline) on both sides of aperture; platinum electrodes on each side

canonical_name: Sysmex hematology analyzer flow cell
creator: Sysmex Corporation (Kobe, Japan)
disclosure_citation: Sysmex Corporation hematology analyzer family (XN-1000, XN-2000, etc.). https://www.sysmex.com
prior_art_notes: Microfluidic flow-cell architecture for clinical hematology counting (CBC differential): Coulter-impedance counting + flow cytometry + reagent mixing on integrated cartridge. Sysmex is the dominant global hematology analyzer vendor with a long history of flow-cell innovation predating the µTAS era. The flow-cell architectures used in modern Sysmex XN-series instruments are direct descendants of 1970s-era Coulter Counter and Technicon SMA designs but at substantially smaller scale.

canonical_name: Videojet Binary Array Continuous Inkjet Coding Printhead
creator: Videojet Technologies Inc. (originally A. B. Dick Company); now part of Veralto
disclosure_citation: Videojet origin as a division of A. B. Dick Co. in the 1960s; binary-array CIJ patents incl. US5523778A 'Binary array ink jet printhead'; current 1280/1520/1580+ datasheets at videojet.com
notable_capabilities: binary deflected CIJ for industrial coding
binary array printhead with parallel droplet paths and per-path charging electrodes
solvent-based inks with closed-loop make-up control
prior_art_notes: Discloses a binary-array CIJ printhead with a single ink chamber feeding multiple parallel orifices, a stimulator producing synchronized break-off across all jets, an electrode assembly with a front face parallel to the droplet paths bearing one charge electrode per path, and a downstream gutter that recovers uncharged drops while charged drops are deflected to substrate. Anticipates: (a) the basic architecture of multi-jet binary CIJ used across industrial coding, (b) per-jet charge electrode placement and addressing for parallel coding without per-jet stimulator electronics, (c) factory-grade CIJ ink-system with viscosity-tracked make-up addition. Predicate to the Videojet 1000 and 1500 product families and the entire packaging-coding CIJ industry alongside Domino, Hitachi, Linx, and Markem-Imaje.

canonical_name: Zoltan/Clevite Squeeze-Tube Drop-on-Demand Piezo Inkjet
creator: Steven I. Zoltan / Clevite Corp.
disclosure_citation: US Patent 3,683,212 'Pulsed droplet ejecting system' issued 1972-08-08 to Steven I. Zoltan, assigned to Clevite Corp.
notable_capabilities: drop-on-demand piezoelectric ejection
tubular acoustic transducer drop generator
prior_art_notes: Discloses an electroacoustic transducer (a radially polarized piezoelectric tube) coupled to liquid in a glass conduit terminating in a small orifice through which discrete droplets are ejected on demand. Anticipates: drop-on-demand piezoelectric inkjet generation in general; specifically (a) using a piezoelectric annulus surrounding an ink-filled cavity to launch a compressive acoustic pulse that breaks off a single droplet at the orifice, (b) electrical pulse-shape control of droplet volume and ejection timing, (c) the architectural pattern of one piezo per nozzle. This is the canonical squeeze-mode (later 'acoustic') piezo inkjet predating Kyser-Sears 1976 bend-mode and the Xaar 1988 shear-mode shared-wall art.
sources: Wijshoff, 'The dynamics of the piezo inkjet printhead operation', Physics Reports 491 (2010) 77–177

canonical_name: Canon thermal Bubble Jet inkjet printhead

creator: Canon Inc., Endo et al.
disclosure_citation: Endo, I.; Sato, Y.; Saito, S.; Nakagiri, T.; Ohno, S. Liquid jet recording process and apparatus therefor. JP S54-59936A (1979); subsequent US patents include US4723129 (1988).
notes: Often forgotten in 'microfluidics' surveys because it predates the µTAS framing. Manz 1990 was new terminology; Canon and HP had been shipping silicon microfluidics for over a decade by then.
prior_art_notes: Foundational disclosure of thermal bubble-jet inkjet printheads — almost certainly the highest-volume microfluidic device ever produced. Anticipates: integrated silicon-based microfluidic channels with embedded thin-film resistive heaters, on-demand vapor-bubble droplet ejection from microscale orifices, and the entire thermal-inkjet category of consumer printers. Microfluidics' largest commercial deployment by orders of magnitude predates the academic field's emergence.

canonical_name: 3M (now Neogen) Petrifilm food microbiology plates

canonical_name: Vaught/Cloutier HP Thermal-Bubble Inkjet Patent (US4490728)
creator: Hewlett-Packard Company
disclosure_citation: US Patent 4,490,728 'Thermal ink jet printer', filed 1981-08-14, issued 1984-12-25, inventors John L. Vaught, Frank L. Cloutier, David K. Donald, John D. Meyer, Christopher A. Tacklind, Howard H. Taub; assignee Hewlett-Packard Company
notable_capabilities: explosive bubble nucleation droplet ejection
two-pulse precursor+nucleation drive scheme
no moving parts in firing chamber
prior_art_notes: Discloses a thermal inkjet printhead that ejects droplets by explosive bubble nucleation in the ink, driven by a thin-film resistor in the ink supply chamber, using a two-part electrical pulse: a precursor pulse that preheats the ink to just below boiling, then a nucleation pulse that drives the resistor to the superheat limit, producing reproducible drop formation. Anticipates: the entire architecture of HP-style thermal inkjet (TIJ); specifically (a) thin-film resistor on silicon as the drop-ejection actuator, (b) precursor+nucleation pulse drive shaping for repeatability and resistor-life extension, (c) integration of ink supply chamber, resistor, and orifice plate as a monolithic die. Companion to the 1979 Endo/Canon thermal disclosure in the existing corpus, and predicate to all HP DeskJet, OfficeJet, and HP PageWide nozzle dies.
sources: Tom's OSU history of HP inkjet, citing American Heritage Invention & Technology

canonical_name: HP ThinkJet thermal inkjet printhead

canonical_name: HemoCue Hb 201+ Capillary Hemoglobin Analyzer

Note: this is a capillary-driven device, NOT an electroosmotic-flow analyzer; it is included to anchor the capillary-fill primitive in the corpus.

canonical_name: Xaar Shared-Wall Shear-Mode Piezo Printhead

notable_capabilities: shared-wall shear-mode actuation

prior_art_notes: Discloses an array of parallel ink channels machined into a block of poled piezoelectric material such that each interior wall is shared between two adjacent channels and is poled so that an applied voltage produces shear-mode deflection that pressurizes the channel on one side and depressurizes the other. Anticipates: the foundational Xaar shared-wall architecture used across the industrial inkjet sector; specifically (a) using piezo block walls themselves as the actuators (no separate diaphragm), (b) cyclic three-phase addressing that fires alternating channels while the others act as electrically grounded references, (c) high nozzle-density per unit length without per-nozzle through-substrate piezo stacks. Predicate to Xaar 128/200/318/500/1001/2001 product families and licensed derivatives.

canonical_name: bioMérieux VIDAS 3 Solid Phase Receptacle (SPR) Immunoassay Cone
creator: bioMérieux
disclosure_citation: bioMérieux VIDAS launch 1990 (pioneering ELFA technology); VIDAS 3 launch 2014; FDA 510(k) K133769
end_application: central- and mid-volume lab Enzyme-Linked Fluorescent Assay (ELFA) immunoassay; particularly clinical microbiology serology, sepsis biomarkers (PCT), and food microbiology pathogen detection
fabrication_method: injection-molded SPR cone with antibody pre-coated on inner surface; sealed reagent strip with 6-10 wells per assay; reel-and-blister assembly
flow_regime: instrument's micropipettor head holds the SPR cone, draws and dispenses sample/reagents through it from each strip well in sequence; 4-methyl-umbelliferyl-phosphate (MUP) substrate cleaved by alkaline phosphatase produces fluorescence read in the last well
notable_capabilities: SPR cone serves as both pipette and solid phase — eliminates separate well-coating steps
single-strip-per-assay format ensuring no carryover
30-minute typical assay time
menu including Procalcitonin, B·R·A·H·M·S PCT, Lyme, Toxoplasma, Hepatitis serology, Salmonella food testing
prior_art_notes: Discloses the bioMérieux SPR (Solid Phase Receptacle) format: a polypropylene cone shaped like a pipette tip whose inner surface is pre-coated with capture antibody; the analyzer's micropipettor docks onto the cone and uses it as both pipette and solid phase, drawing sample and reagents in/out from a sealed reagent strip with 6-10 pre-loaded wells (sample well, wash wells, conjugate well, substrate well). Anticipates: integrated pipette-as-solid-phase fluidic primitive eliminating separate microtiter plate coating; sealed reagent strips with foil seal pierced by the SPR mating action; ELFA (Enzyme-Linked Fluorescent Assay) using MUP→4-methylumbelliferone for sub-pg/mL sensitivity in a single-strip format. Foundational architectural disclosure dating to 1990 — relevant prior art for many subsequent disposable-cartridge-with-pipette-cone architectures (e.g., Biotech / VIDAS-derivative platforms).
sources: VIDAS PCT IFU; US patent 5,147,609 (bioMérieux SPR)
substrate_material: Solid Phase Receptacle (SPR) — pipette-tip-shaped antibody-coated polypropylene cone; reagent strip (foiled blister wells with reagents, wash buffer, fluorogenic substrate)

canonical_name: OLS Bio CASY Cell Counter and Analyzer (formerly Innovatis CASY-TT)
creator: OLS Bio (formerly Innovatis AG; Roche Diagnostics divestiture)
disclosure_citation: Innovatis (Bielefeld, Germany) CASY launch 1991; CASY-TT (TwinTechnology) launch 2006; Innovatis acquired by Roche 2008; CASY product line now sold by OLS-Bio (since 2013); Pulsar Coulter-principle patent extension
end_application: bioprocess cell counting + viability (live/dead via volumetric discrimination, no stain) for mammalian, insect, microbial cultures
fabrication_method: precision-drilled glass aperture in cuvette block; piezo-pulsed pressure-driven sample transport; constant-DC current source + low-noise amplifier
flow_regime: Coulter-principle electrical sensing zone (50 µm, 60 µm, or 150 µm aperture options); pulse-area integration measurement (Pulse Area Analysis, PAA) — instead of the conventional Coulter peak-amplitude detection, the CASY integrates the pulse over time, yielding cell volume even for cells with non-conductive interiors (live cells with intact membrane have inflated effective volume vs dead cells with disrupted membrane)
notable_capabilities: stain-free live/dead discrimination via Pulse Area Analysis
particle size distribution from 0.7 µm to 200+ µm in single measurement
industrial particle sizing extension (paints, ceramic powders)
5000 cells/sec throughput
prior_art_notes: Discloses the CASY Pulse Area Analysis variant of Coulter-principle particle counting: instead of peak-amplitude pulse detection (which conflates fast-transit small particles with slow-transit large particles), the CASY integrates each impedance pulse over time, yielding a true volume measurement; importantly, intact cell membranes block the electrolyte from penetrating the cell interior, so live cells appear to have their full hydrodynamic volume, while dead cells with permeabilized membranes appear shrunken to nuclear volume — providing label-free live/dead discrimination. Anticipates: stain-free viability discrimination via electrical sensing zone integration; the architectural choice of Pulse Area Analysis vs amplitude detection in Coulter-derivative instruments; the use of multiple aperture sizes (50, 60, 150 µm) in a single instrument enabling 0.7-200 µm dynamic range in one measurement. Important historical anchor for the bioprocess cell counting market dominated by image cytometry (Vi-CELL) and impedance (CASY) before flow cytometry routine.
sources: Lindl, T. et al. ALTEX 22:142-147 (2005), CASY method evaluation
substrate_material: precision-drilled glass capillary aperture (typically 60-200 µm); CASYton electrolyte buffer; CASYclean wash; cell suspension diluted 1:200 in electrolyte

canonical_name: Haemonetics TEG 6s Thromboelastography Microfluidic Cartridge

flow_regime: user adds 360 µL whole blood through port; capillary distribution to 4 wells; cartridge mechanical resonance excitation by piezo at 0.06 Hz; clot formation increases mechanical coupling between cartridge wall and blood meniscus, shifting resonance frequency detected optically
notable_capabilities: 4 simultaneous viscoelastic assays from one 360 µL whole blood sample
no operator pipetting (single port load)

vibration-tolerant resonance detection (suitable for OR/ER environment)
prior_art_notes: Discloses a microfluidic cartridge-based viscoelastic hemostasis analyzer using mechanical resonance frequency detection rather than the historic torque-pin method (TEG 5000, ROTEM): the cartridge is excited by piezoelectric driver at ~0.06 Hz; an LED illuminates the blood-air meniscus inside each microwell; clot formation increases mechanical coupling between the resonating cartridge wall and the meniscus, modulating the meniscus position which is detected by photodiode displacement sensor — yielding a TEG-equivalent amplitude trace (R, K, alpha, MA) without any moving torque pin in the blood. Anticipates: cartridge-resident viscoelastic hemostasis testing eliminating the cup-and-pin mechanism; the architectural choice of resonance-shift detection enabling vibration tolerance suitable for transport / cardiac OR. Distinct from ROTEM sigma (Werfen) which uses electromechanical detection in a similar cartridge format.
substrate_material: polycarbonate microfluidic cartridge with 4 reagent-pre-loaded reaction wells (Kaolin TEG, Kaolin TEG with Heparinase, RapidTEG, Functional Fibrinogen); blood inlet port; LED + photodiode optical-resonance read window

prior_art_notes: Combinatorial split-pool barcoding kit derived from the SPLiT-seq method (Rosenberg & Roco 2018). Also anticipates instrument-side passive fluidic handling consisting solely of plate transfer and centrifugation.
